entry: Fall in blood sugar to levels below normal, also called low blood sugar and typically below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Symptoms may include headache, tiredness, confusion, shakiness, seizures, loss of consciousness, or death. The most common cause is diabetes medication such as [[Insulin]], and risk is higher for people with diabetes who eat less than usual, exercise or drink alcohol. Other causes include severe illness, [[Sepsis]], kidney failure and liver disease. Treatment is a fast-acting sugary food or drink, such as glucose tablets or apple juice; when a person cannot take food by mouth, glucagon by injection may help.

Drop in human core body temperature below 35.0 °C (95.0 °F). Mild hypothermia causes shivering and mental confusion. In moderate cases shivering stops and confusion increases, and in severe cases hallucinations, paradoxical undressing and an increased risk of the heart stopping may occur. It classically results from exposure to cold weather or cold-water immersion, but any condition that reduces heat production or increases heat loss can cause it, including [[Alcohol intoxication|alcohol intoxication]], low blood sugar, [[Anorexia]] and advanced age. Mild cases are treated with warm drinks and clothing, moderate cases with heating blankets and warmed intravenous fluids, and severe cases may require extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or cardiopulmonary bypass. Hypothermia causes at least 1,500 deaths a year in the United States alone. The name derives from Greek words meaning under and heat.

Proposed explanation for a phenomenon. A scientific hypothesis must be based on observations and make a testable, reproducible prediction about reality, beginning as an educated guess. If experiments repeatedly and independently show it to be true, it becomes a [[Scientific theory|scientific theory]]; in everyday use the two words are often interchanged, which is incorrect in science. A working hypothesis is provisionally accepted to advance research and is often discarded. In formal logic, a hypothesis is the antecedent of a proposition: in the proposition "If P, then Q", P is the hypothesis. [[Karl Popper]] argued that a hypothesis must be falsifiable, meaning it can be shown to be false.

Endocrine disease marked by insufficient [[Thyroid|thyroid]] hormone production. Symptoms include poor tolerance of cold, extreme fatigue, muscle aches, constipation, slow heart rate, depression and weight gain. Worldwide, too little dietary [[Iodine|iodine]] is the most common cause; where iodine intake is sufficient, the usual cause is Hashimoto's thyroiditis, an [[Autoimmune disease|autoimmune disease]]. Diagnosis uses blood tests of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and thyroxine (T4). Treatment is levothyroxine, a thyroid hormone replacement, with doses adjusted to symptoms and TSH levels. Overt hypothyroidism affects about 0.3–0.4% of people in the United States and is more common in women.

Insufficient [[Oxygen|oxygen]] supply at the tissue level, affecting the whole body or a local region. Hypoxia differs from hypoxemia and anoxemia, which refer specifically to low or absent oxygen in the blood. It may have external causes, such as breathing a low-oxygen gas, or internal ones, such as reduced gas transfer in the [[Lung|lungs]], reduced ability of the blood to carry oxygen, or poor blood flow. People who ascend to high altitude develop generalized hypoxia, which can cause high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) and high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE). It is also a common complication of preterm birth, because premature infants often have underdeveloped lungs; they may be placed in incubators with supplemental oxygen, and serious cases receive continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP).

Small, stout, herbivorous mammal of the order Hyracoidea, also called a dassie. Hyraxes are well-furred and typically 30–70 cm (12–28 in) long, weighing 2–5 kg (4–11 lb). Although they resemble marmots or large pikas, they are more closely related to [[Elephant|elephants]] and [[Sirenia|sirenians]]. Their lifespan is 9 to 14 years. Almost all species are limited to [[Africa]]; the exception, the rock hyrax, also lives in adjacent parts of the [[Middle East]]. Hyraxes compensate for poorly developed internal temperature regulation by huddling and basking in the sun. Their upper incisors grow continuously, and their multichambered stomachs break down tough plant material. Females give birth to up to four young after a gestation of seven to eight months. Hyraxes live in small family groups led by a single male that defends the territory.

Dependence of a system's state on its history. A magnet, for example, may have more than one possible magnetic moment in a given field, depending on how the field changed in the past. This memory effect underlies data storage in a [[Hard disk drive]] and the remanence that keeps a record of Earth's magnetic field in the past. Hysteresis occurs in [[Ferromagnetism|ferromagnetic]] materials, rubber bands and shape-memory alloys, and is often linked to irreversible change and internal friction. Thermostats use it to prevent unwanted frequent switching. The term was coined in 1881 by Sir James Alfred Ewing, from an Ancient Greek word meaning lagging behind.

Term for ungovernable emotional excess, formerly a medical diagnosis mainly applied to women. In the 19th century female hysteria was considered a diagnosable physical illness; in the 20th it came to be treated as a mental illness. [[Sigmund Freud]] and Jean-Martin Charcot studied hysteria patients. Most physicians no longer accept it as a medical diagnosis. The word comes from the Ancient Greek for uterus. The oldest record, from 1900 BCE in ancient Egypt, describes behavior attributed to a wandering uterus. The diagnosis has since been divided into categories including [[Epilepsy]], [[Histrionic personality disorder|histrionic personality disorder]] and conversion disorders.

American multinational technology company, headquartered in Armonk, New York. Founded in 1911 as the Computing-Tabulating-Recording Company, it was renamed International Business Machines in 1924 and became a leading manufacturer of punch-card tabulating systems. Its System/360 mainframe family dominated computing in the 1960s and 1970s, when the company produced 80 percent of computers in the United States. The [[Personal computer|IBM Personal Computer]], introduced in 1981, set an architecture that remains the basis for most personal computers. IBM sold its microcomputer division to [[Lenovo]] in 2005 and afterward concentrated on services, software and supercomputers. It held the record for most annual U.S. patents by a business for 29 consecutive years, from 1993 to 2021. Its innovations include the [[Floppy disk|floppy disk]], the [[Hard disk drive]] and the SQL programming language. In 1997 its [[Supercomputer|supercomputer]] Deep Blue defeated [[Garry Kasparov]] at chess.

[[Sweden|Swedish]] multinational conglomerate selling ready-to-assemble [[Furniture|furniture]] and household goods. Founded in 1943 by Ingvar Kamprad, IKEA has been the world's largest furniture retailer since 2008. Its name is an acronym of Kamprad's initials, his family farm Elmtaryd and his hometown Agunnaryd. It is known for modernist design, low prices and large showroom-style stores. Its operational hub is in Älmhult, Sweden, where the first store opened in 1958. More than 500 stores operate in 60 countries and three territories, and €45.1 billion worth of goods were sold in fiscal year 2024. The IKEA brand is owned by Inter IKEA Systems B.V., based in the [[Netherlands]].

Online database of information on films, television series, video games and streaming content. Entries include cast and crew, plot summaries, trivia, ratings and reviews. As of September 2025 it contained some 25.9 million titles and 14.8 million person records, and it ranked as the 40th most visited website in the world. Its Top 250 list is based on ratings from regular registered voters, and *The Shawshank Redemption* has been the highest-ranked film since 2008. Known originally as the Internet Movie Database, it has been owned by [[Amazon (company)|Amazon]] since 1998.

Mobile operating system developed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] for the [[IPhone|iPhone]] line. Launched in June 2007 as iPhone OS, it is the basis of iPadOS, tvOS and watchOS. It is the world's second most widely installed mobile operating system after [[Android (operating system)|Android]]. Based on macOS, it is a Unix-like system with components of the Mach microkernel and FreeBSD, though most of it is proprietary. The App Store contained more than 3.8 million iOS apps as of December 2023.

Numerical label assigned to a device on a computer network that uses the [[Internet Protocol]]. IP addresses serve two functions: identifying a network interface and giving the device's location so that a path can be established. [[IPv4]] addresses are 32-bit numbers in use since 1983. Their shortage led to the designated successor, [[IPv6]], which uses 128-bit addresses. Addresses are allocated through the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) and five regional Internet registries, and network administrators assign them to devices statically or dynamically. Some jurisdictions, such as [[Canada]] and the [[European Union]], consider IP addresses personal data.

Line of tablet computers developed and marketed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] since 2010. The first-generation iPad was introduced on January 27, 2010. The line has since expanded to the smaller iPad Mini, the lighter iPad Air and the flagship iPad Pro. The original device ran a variant of [[IOS|iOS]], and since September 2019 iPads have used iPadOS, a fork with a user interface tailored to larger screens. Over 670 million iPads had been sold as of 2022, making Apple the largest vendor of tablet computers. The iPad is used in business, education and healthcare.

Line of smartphones developed and marketed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] since 2007. [[Steve Jobs]] announced the first-generation iPhone on January 9, 2007, and it launched on June 29, 2007, at US$499. It was the first mobile phone to use multi-touch technology and is credited with popularizing the slate smartphone form factor and a large market for smartphone apps. Its operating system is [[IOS|iOS]], one of the two major smartphone platforms alongside [[Android (operating system)|Android]]. Later models added Retina displays, video recording and waterproofing. Touch ID fingerprint sensors appeared with the iPhone 5s, and from the iPhone X onward Face ID replaced Touch ID for authentication. More than three billion iPhones had been sold as of July 2025, and Apple has been the largest mobile phone vendor since 2023.

Line of portable media players by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]], sold from 2001 to 2022. The first iPod was released on November 10, 2001, about ten months after the Macintosh version of [[ITunes|iTunes]]. Apple sold an estimated 450 million iPods. Apple discontinued the line on May 10, 2022, and it was the longest-running product Apple had discontinued, with a lifespan of over 20 years. During the middle of 2010, iPhone sales overtook those of the iPod.

First standalone specification of the [[Internet Protocol]], still used to carry much of the Internet's traffic. It was first deployed on the [[ARPANET]] in January 1983 and uses 32-bit addresses, giving 4,294,967,296 unique values. IPv4 is connectionless and offers best-effort delivery, so reliability is handled by protocols such as the [[Transmission Control Protocol]]. As the Internet grew the pool of addresses ran short, and on February 3, 2011, IANA allocated the last five blocks in its free pool. Its successor is [[IPv6]], which uses 128-bit addresses.

Most recent version of the [[Internet Protocol]], developed by the Internet Engineering Task Force to overcome [[IPv4]] address exhaustion. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, giving 2¹²⁸ (approximately 3.4×10³⁸) possible values. Addresses are written as eight groups of four [[Hexadecimal|hexadecimal]] digits separated by colons. IPv6 is not backwards-compatible with IPv4, although transition mechanisms allow the two to coexist. It supports unicast, anycast and multicast transmission but has no broadcast addresses. It became an Internet Standard on July 14, 2017.

International Standard Book Number, a numeric commercial identifier for [[Book|books]]. Publishers obtain ISBNs from an affiliate of the International ISBN Agency. A different ISBN is assigned to each edition or variation, such as an e-book and a paperback, but an unchanged reprint keeps its ISBN. ISBNs assigned before 2007 have ten digits, and those assigned on or after January 1, 2007 have thirteen. The format was published as ISO 2108 in 1970, adapting the nine-digit Standard Book Number (SBN) of 1966. The ISSN identifies periodicals such as magazines and newspapers.

National space agency of [[India]], headquartered in [[Bengaluru]], Karnataka. Formerly the Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR), set up in 1962, it was renamed ISRO in 1969. The agency operates satellites for imaging, communications and [[Remote sensing|remote sensing]], and navigation systems such as GAGAN and NavIC. It has sent three missions to the [[Moon]] and one to [[Mars]]. Its first satellite, [[Aryabhata]], was launched by the Soviet agency Interkosmos in 1975. In 1980 India became the seventh country to achieve orbital launches. ISRO also supports disaster management, telemedicine and navigation.

American influencer, entrepreneur and online streamer known as IShowSpeed. Born in [[Cincinnati]], Ohio, he began posting gaming content on [[YouTube]] after registering his channel in 2016. He gained attention in 2021 for dramatic reactions to games, then shifted toward general entertainment and soccer content, often centered on his support for [[Cristiano Ronaldo]]. From 2024 he livestreamed tours of countries around the world. He released the single "World Cup" in 2022 with Warner Records and was named Breakout Streamer of the Year at the 12th Streamy Awards.

Media player and media library software developed by [[Apple Inc.|Apple]] for Windows and, formerly, macOS. Apple announced it on January 9, 2001, and it began as a music library and player for Mac users. The 2003 addition of the iTunes Store for downloading digital music, and a Windows version that year, made it the main tool for managing [[IPod|iPod]] players and later the [[IPhone|iPhone]] and [[IPad|iPad]]. Support for video, podcasts and mobile apps followed. In October 2019 Apple replaced iTunes on macOS with the Music, Podcasts and TV apps, and in February 2024 most Windows features were split among other apps.

Stage name of Lee Ji-eun, South Korean singer-songwriter and actress. She debuted as a singer at fifteen with the EP *Lost and Found* (2008). Her national breakthrough came with the 2010 single "Good Day", which spent five consecutive weeks at number one on South Korea's Gaon Digital Chart. Her 2020 single "Eight" was her first to top Billboard's World Digital Song Sales chart. Her roles in *My Mister* (2018) and *When Life Gives You Tangerines* (2025) earned critical acclaim. She has released five studio albums and thirty-one number-one singles, the most of any artist in South Korea.

Ancient Chinese divination text, also called *Book of Changes*, and among the oldest Chinese classics. Originally a divination manual of the [[Zhou dynasty|Western Zhou period]], it was expanded during the Warring States and early imperial periods with philosophical commentaries known as the Ten Wings. After becoming part of the Chinese Five Classics in the 2nd century BC, it was the basis of divination for centuries across the Far East. Divination uses bundles of yarrow stalks to produce sets of six numbers from 6 to 9, and each of the 64 possible sets corresponds to a hexagram. Commentators have read the text as moral guidance informed by [[Confucianism]], [[Taoism]] and [[Buddhism]], and the hexagrams have been linked to [[Yin and yang|yin and yang]] and other cosmological ideas.

entry: Post-apocalyptic science fiction horror short story by Harlan Ellison, first published in the March 1967 issue of *IF: Worlds of Science Fiction*. Set during a nuclear World War III between the [[Soviet Union]], [[United States]] and [[China]], it centers on the Allied Mastercomputer (AM), an [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] that kills nearly all of humanity. AM keeps five survivors alive underground, torturing them and denying them death. The story won a Hugo Award in 1968 and inspired a 1995 computer game co-authored by Ellison and a BBC Radio 4 play.
